papers.title: Agent Identity and Authority: A Research Framework for Evaluating Enforceable Security Boundaries in Autonomous AI Systems
papers.summary: The Agent Identity and Authority Lab (AIAL) is an independent cybersecurity research initiative examining the effectiveness of enforceable identity, delegated authority, and authorization controls for autonomous AI agents. This pre-experimental research proposal establishes a framework for evaluating the distinction between behavioral guardrails and independently enforced security boundaries. The proposed research investigates agent identity, least-privilege authorization, persistent memory, historical permissions, tool access, policy enforcement, revocation, and auditability. Controlled experiments will compare prompt-based restrictions with externally enforced authorization mechanisms using simulated enterprise resources and synthetic data. The initiative aims to produce reproducible evidence that can inform AI agent security architecture, enterprise governance practices, and ongoing industry standards discussions, including relevant NIST and OWASP initiatives. This publication presents the research framework and proposed methodology. It does not claim completed experimental validation.

papers.title: Persistent Semantic Agency: An Architecture for Agent Systems Beyond the Loop
papers.summary: Persistent Semantic Agency argues that the architectural center of an intelligent agent system must move from the trajectory of a model to a persistent semantic system of delegated commitments, structured work, knowledge, memory, responsibility, authority, and evidence. Models reason inside that system; they do not constitute it. This technical manifesto and reference architecture develops a domain-independent model for long-horizon agent systems. It introduces Commitment as the unit of durable agency; a typed semantic Work Intermediate Representation (Work IR); explicit Unknowns, Decisions, Responsibility, Delegation, Authority, and Evidence; a strict separation of Memory, Knowledge, State, and Context; dynamic composition of models, humans, solvers, compilers, knowledge sources, and organizations as cognitive and execution Resources; and proposal/admission, independent observation, verification, acceptance, and derived Closure as the governing transition model. The publication comprises fourteen chapters and sixteen architectural figures. It situates the proposal against planning theory, hierarchical planning, truth maintenance, cognitive architectures, distributed cognition, provenance, capability security, graph engineering, long-term memory, and contemporary agent systems. It concludes with worked examples, falsification tests, and canonical definitions. The individual mec

papers.title: An evaluation guided multiagent framework for generating floor plans that comply with municipal building regulations
papers.summary: Abstract Generative models often produce perceptually plausible outputs that violate hard domain rules. In architectural layout generation, balancing geometric intuition with regulatory compliance remains a persistent challenge, as current frameworks routinely fail to conform to local building laws. This paper proposes LayoutGen, a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework coupling probabilistic generation with deterministic verification in an evaluation-guided refinement loop. LayoutGen employs a four-phase retrieval-driven pipeline (spatial reasoning, coordinate mapping, vector rendering, and iterative refinement) powered by a dual retrieval engine leveraging architectural precedents and legislative laws. An Evaluation Engine scores the generated 2D Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) layouts and returns a graded, itemised report. Every scored quantity is computed by deterministic geometric checks over the generated coordinates against a structured rule repository; the Large Language Model (LLM) is confined to spatial planning, coordinate proposal, and the natural language feedback that drives refinement, together with an advisory Vaastu commentary that does not enter the grade. Evaluated on single-storey residential configurations drawn from the RPLAN and MSD datasets, spanning studio to 3BHK typologies and represented as axisaligned rectangular rooms, the full pipeline reduces detect

papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluat

papers.title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. papers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
papers.summary: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with

papers.title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to intervene with a high-cost slow path. To unlock its steering intelligence, the ability to assess goal drift and generate effective interventions, we jointly train the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.

papers.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
papers.summary: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and el

papers.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
papers.summary: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. papers.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
papers.summary: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their m

papers.title: From utterances to actionable labels: Toward practical and scalable open intent discovery in production systems
papers.summary: This thesis presents novel contributions to the field of Open Intent Discovery (OID), addressing fundamental challenges in the unsupervised identification and labelling of user intents within unlabelled datasets. Existing work in OID often relies on small, static, and clean datasets, lacks robust methods for generating interpretable intent labels, and exhibits inconsistencies in evaluation methodologies. This research responds to these gaps by introducing a modular, fully unsupervised framework that supports the complete OID pipeline, from clustering to label generation, without requiring labelled data or large-scale pre-trained language models. A key academic contribution is the development of a fine-grained intent labelling technique based on an enhanced Action-Object extraction method. This method incorporates compound noun and adjective structures to improve the expressiveness and semantic precision of generated labels. The framework enables systematic comparison across different OID configurations, revealing how dataset properties such as utterance length, vocabulary diversity, and intent structure influence algorithm performance. Furthermore, a configuration prediction module is introduced to explore the feasibility of automating technique selection based on dataset features. Comprehensive experiments on both public and complex real-world datasets demonstrate the adaptabi

papers.title: Beyond Task Delegation: Reconceptualising Instructional Design to Measure Competence in the Age of Generative AI
papers.summary: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has invalidated traditional content-recall assessments, acting as a catalyst for a systemic transition towards Competence-Based Education (CBE). This paper contends that the role of faculty must transcend content dissemination, focusing instead on observable human competencies associated with Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL). Drawing upon Behaviourism and Bloom's Taxonomy, we propose the Reverse-Flipped Model. This conceptual framework, supported by illustrative disciplinary cases in History, Computer Science, Digital Photography, and Composition, utilises generative tools for low-stakes production to repurpose pedagogical time for high-stakes human intervention. Prompt Literacy is conceptualised as an observable instructional competency that externalises planning, monitoring, evaluation, and strategic intervention behaviours during human-AI collaboration. Implementation necessitates the use of Analytic Rubrics and Automated Process Portfolios (APP) to document observable demonstrations of Prompt Literacy and strategic engagement over final product quality. The framework addresses institutional sustainability and the moral imperative of digital equity. The primary contribution of this framework is a structural shift that enhances assessment validity by ensuring student success is defined by verifiable master

papers.title: Schizophrenia research in 2026: report from the annual meeting of the Schizophrenia International Research Society
papers.summary: Abstract SIRS 2026, held under the theme “Schizophrenia Research in the Era of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together researchers, clinicians, and persons with lived experience to take stock of a field whose tools for measuring, predicting, and intervening in psychosis have expanded rapidly. Themes spanned artificial intelligence, automated speech analysis, retinal imaging, computational modelling, and novel psychosocial and pharmacological targets, with evidence that, individually, warrants cautious but serious attention and that, collectively, points toward a more mechanistically grounded psychiatry. A recurring call across the meeting was for rigorous external validation, equitable implementation, and sustained scrutiny of underlying assumptions, including whether existing diagnostic categories and treatment targets remain adequate. Some areas remained underworked relative to their importance, including translating basic neuroscience advances into questions relevant to patients and families, and the structural determinants of illness onset and treatment access. Perhaps the most significant development at SIRS 2026 was not any single scientific finding but the broadening of whose voices and experiences are treated as evidence worth taking seriously in this era of AI, a shift whose consolidation remains a question for the field as much as for any individual programme of wo

papers.title: Fragmented control, collective risk: multi‐agent AI and the coming governance crisis
papers.summary: Abstract Multi‐agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) systems are increasingly deployed across economic and digital infrastructures. Existing regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act and related initiatives, largely focus on individual AI systems and are therefore poorly suited to govern risks that arise from agent interaction. This paper argues that multi‐agent AI introduces distinct governance challenges, including emergent behavior, tacit coordination, cascading systemic risks, and difficulties in assigning accountability. Traditional risk management approaches, which rely on static and component‐based analysis, are inadequate for adaptive, networked systems operating across jurisdictions. Through a comparative review of policy developments in the European Union, United States, and Asia‐Pacific region, the paper identifies a growing governance gap, alongside early regulatory experimentation such as China's emerging standards for intelligent agents. The paper concludes that effective oversight will require a shift from model‐centric regulation toward system‐level and adaptive governance frameworks capable of addressing the collective dynamics of multi‐agent AI systems.

papers.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
papers.summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or li

papers.title: Talking with language models
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) produce text that invites us to treat our interactions with them as conversations, and to treat them as intelligent interlocutors who remember, act, and make commitments. We argue that this conversational presupposition is mistaken. We introduce the artifactual stance, which describes human–AI interaction in terms of their design and affordances, rather than potential intentional attitudes. On our account, LLMs produce candidate text that users interpret, evaluate, and sometimes adopt as their own speech. We argue that such exchanges are not conversations, since generating text does not itself constitute an utterance or the performance of a speech act. Rather the communicative and normative work of interpretation, commitment, and action remains with the user. Our framework explains both the sophistication and usefulness of LLMs, and the conversational appearances that can be traced back to properties of the interface and to artifact design. It also reframes puzzles about AI reference, the persistence of supposed interlocutors, and responsibility for AI-generated text. These questions are better approached through an account of how artifacts mediate human linguistic practices than through assumptions about AI speakerhood.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management: A Systematic Literature Review, Integrative Framework, and Future Research Agenda
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping Human Resource Management (HRM) by transforming how organizations acquire, develop, deploy, evaluate, and retain human capital while expanding HR’s strategic role in decision-making and value creation. Despite growing scholarly attention, AI-driven HRM research remains fragmented across HR functions, theoretical perspectives, technological capabilities, and organizational contexts, limiting understanding of how AI creates value, through which mechanisms it influences employee and organizational outcomes, and under what conditions these effects emerge. This study addresses these limitations through a systematic literature review of research on AI-driven HRM published between 2011 and 1 July 2026. The review critically synthesizes the evolution, applications, enabling capabilities, value-creation mechanisms, implementation conditions, and outcomes of AI-driven HRM, with particular attention to human–AI collaboration, organizational readiness, leadership, organizational culture, AI literacy, employee trust, workforce adaptability, and responsible AI governance. It identifies key conceptual, theoretical, empirical, methodological, and contextual gaps and develops a structured agenda for future research. Building on the synthesized evidence, the study proposes an integrative framework that conceptualizes AI-driven HRM as a dynamic socio-tech

papers.title: Integrating multi-layer digital twins into engineering education: a design-based research framework for industry 4.0 competency development
papers.summary: This study presents a Design-Based Research (DBR) framework integrating Digital Twin development into undergraduate engineering education through Project-Based Learning. Sixty students across eighteen teams worked in project teams toward a multi-layer Digital Twin architecture for a manufacturing process, spanning process analysis, discrete-event simulation (Siemens Tecnomatix Plant Simulation), three-dimensional validation (Process Simulate/CAD), SCADA visualization (Node-RED, Firebase), and AI-assisted decision support (Gemini API); all 18 teams completed the process-analysis through 3D-validation stages, while 15/18 teams completed the SCADA stage and 16/18 completed the AI-assisted decision-support stage within the available course timeframe. Competency assessment using a structured rubric ( κ = 0.78 inter-rater reliability) indicated that students demonstrated systems thinking, simulation modeling, industrial automation, and evidence-based decision-making. Cohort-level simulation outputs ranged from 720 to 850 units (mean = 789, SD = 38), with 14/18 teams identifying common capacity-mismatch challenges. The framework offers a potentially adaptable model for integrating Industry 4.0 technologies into engineering curricula, preparing students for the technological and human-centered challenges of contemporary manufacturing.

Artificial Intelligence Use in Honours Research: Implications for Supervision Relationships, Knowledge Development, and Research Quality
papers.summary: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has reshaped how students engage with academic research, particularly at Honours level, where students transition from structured undergraduate learning to independent postgraduate research. Guided by Self‑Regulated Learning (SRL) theory, this study examines how reliance on AI by Honours research students influences the supervisor-supervisee relationship, the quality of research produced, and the extent of knowledge gained through the research process. SRL theory emphasises learners’ ability to plan, monitor, and reflect on their own learning, which is central to successful postgraduate research development. This study adopts a conceptual and literature‑based review methodology, drawing on peer‑reviewed studies on AI use in higher education, literature on postgraduate supervision, and academic integrity and research skills development frameworks, with specific attention to Honours‑level contexts. The documents were analysed using thematic content analysis, focusing on self‑regulatory behaviours, supervisory interaction, research skill development, and learning depth. The findings suggest that limited and transparent use of AI can support honours students by reducing surface‑level cognitive load and assisting with language clarity. However, excessive reliance on AI may undermine key self‑regulation proc

papers.title: VP-EVT: Active Visibility Preservation for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.summary: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the ret

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: T-cell recognition of SARS-CoV-2 antigen peptides following booster vaccination with mRNA and viral-vectored COVID-19 vaccines
papers.summary: Background Durability and breadth of SARS-CoV-2-specific T-cell responses following booster vaccination remain key to guiding next-generation vaccine design, especially in the context of waning antibodies, emerging variants, and diverse immunological backgrounds. This longitudinal study assessed IFN-γ-producing T-cell responses in 46 fully vaccinated adults who received a booster dose of either the BNT162b2 (mRNA) or Ad26.COV2.S (adenoviral vector) vaccine. All participants were nucleocapsid-seropositive at baseline, with antibody levels stable throughout follow-up, indicating prior natural infection and no incident infection during the study period. Methods Using an ex vivo IFN-γ ELISpot assay, responses were measured at four timepoints (baseline, Months 3, 6 and 9) against spike (S; n = 46) and nucleocapsid (N; n = 16) peptides selected by NetMHCpan-4.1 prediction from overlapping 15-mer libraries spanning both proteins. Each peptide was tested individually, allowing every response to be assigned to a defined sequence. Longitudinal change was modelled using linear mixed-effects models, comparing total with median per-peptide responses to distinguish loss of specificities from loss of per-epitope strength. Analyses were stratified by booster type and vaccination strategy (homologous vs. heterologous). Results Time strongly affected total S-specific IFN-γ responses (F(3, 96.6)

papers.title: AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and v

papers.title: Using AI to Build Student Feedback Literacy and Leverage Assessment as a Learning Tool
papers.summary: This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

papers.title: Playing the devil’s advocate: A pathway to stronger critical thinking skills
papers.summary: Saudi Arabian college students may face challenges in developing critical thinking skills, which are considered essential for the future workforce under Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 initiative. The present study used a quasi-experimental design to test the effectiveness of the Devil’s Advocate approach in improving critical thinking among Saudi undergraduates. Forty-three students enrolled in two equivalent course sections were assigned to an experimental group (n = 22) employing the Devil’s Advocate method or a control group (n = 21) engaging in traditional consensus-oriented discussion across a 15-week semester. Critical thinking was assessed at pretest and posttest using the California Critical Thinking Skills Test Form 2000 (CCTST; Insight Assessment, 2013), yielding scores on five reasoning domains (Analysis, Inference, Evaluation, Induction, and Deduction) and an Overall composite score. Independent-samples t-tests confirmed baseline equivalence (all p > .65). Within the experimental group, paired-samples t-tests revealed statistically significant and very large gains on every domain (Cohen's d = 1.64-2.15, all p < .001), whereas the control group showed only small, non-significant changes. ANCOVA controlling for pretest scores confirmed that the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group on every outcome, with large effect sizes (partial η² = .324-.445

papers.title: When Correctness Feedback Erases Evidence: Phase-Separated Completeness Auditing in Verus
papers.summary: Correctness feedback suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing is designed to uncover: programs that satisfy a written contract but violate intended behavior. We demonstrate this objective reversal on 12 Verus/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets. Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to INTENTSHIELD’s corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: Synergistic strategies of tumor ablation and immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma: mechanisms, clinical translation, and perspectives
papers.summary: Abstract Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, accounting for over 85% of primary liver cancers. Locoregional ablation techniques—encompassing thermal modalities such as radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and microwave ablation (MWA), and non-thermal approaches including cryoablation (CA) and irreversible electroporation (IRE)—have been established as standard-of-care options for early-stage HCC. Ablation induces immunogenic cell death (ICD), releasing tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that prime antitumor immunity; however, this response is transient and insufficient to overcome the immunosuppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), necessitating combination with immunotherapy. While preclinical evidence supports ablation-immunotherapy synergy across multiple platforms, robust phase III clinical data demonstrating survival benefit remain limited.
